Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

The Acme Projects API lets you create, list, update and archive projects, manage project members, and subscribe to webhooks for project lifecycle events. If you are coming from the legacy `/api/projects.json` endpoints, read the [migration notes](https://docs.acme.example.com/guides/migrating-from-legacy-api?utm_source=api-reference&utm_medium=docs&utm_campaign=v1-launch#mapping-old-fields-to-new-fields) first: several field names changed, `?page=` is gone, and archived projects are no longer returned by default.

> [!NOTE]
> This reference covers **v1** only. Endpoints marked _beta_ may change without a
> deprecation period; everything else follows the [versioning policy][versioning].

## Contents

* [Authentication](#authentication)
* [Conventions](#conventions)
    * [Pagination](#pagination)
    * [Rate limits](#rate-limits)
    * [Errors](#errors)
* [Projects](#projects)
* [Members](#members)
* [Webhooks](#webhooks-beta)
* [Status codes](#status-codes)

## Authentication ##

Every request must carry a bearer token in the `Authorization` header. Tokens are created in
the dashboard under **Settings → API tokens** and are scoped: a token that only has
`projects:read` cannot create, modify or archive anything.

```http
GET /v1/projects HTTP/1.1
Host: api.acme.example.com
Authorization: Bearer acme_pat_2f9c1d7e8b4a40c6a1d3e5f7
Accept: application/json
```

Scopes
:   `projects:read` — list and fetch projects and members
:   `projects:write` — create, update and archive projects
:   `members:admin` — invite and remove members, change roles

Personal tokens don't expire on their own, but they are revoked after **90 days without use**.  
Service accounts should use the OAuth 2.0 client-credentials flow instead, see
<https://docs.acme.example.com/auth/client-credentials>.

Conventions
-----------

### Pagination

List endpoints are cursor-paginated. Pass `limit` (1–100, default 20) and, for every following page, the `next_cursor` value from the previous response as `cursor`. Cursors are opaque base64 strings — please don't decode them, the format has changed twice already and it will change again. When `has_more` is `false` you have reached the end and `next_cursor` is `null`. Cursors expire after 24 hours; an expired cursor returns `410 Gone` with code `cursor_expired`.

```json
{
  "data": [
    { "id": "prj_01HV3Q4ZK8", "name": "Website relaunch" },
    { "id": "prj_01HQ9ZT1AA", "name": "Template: client project" }
  ],
  "has_more": true,
  "next_cursor": "eyJpZCI6InByal8wMUhROVpUMUFBIn0="
}
```

### Rate limits
Each token gets 600 requests per minute with a burst of 100. Every response carries:

`X-RateLimit-Limit`
:   Requests allowed in the current window.

`X-RateLimit-Remaining`
:   Requests left in the current window. At `0` you get `429 Too Many Requests`.

`X-RateLimit-Reset`
:   Unix timestamp (seconds) at which the window resets.

`Retry-After`
:   Only on `429` responses. Seconds to wait before retrying. Please honour it —
    clients that keep hammering the API after a 429 are blocked for ten minutes.

### Errors

Errors share one envelope. `error.code` is stable and safe to switch on; `error.message` is meant for humans and can change at any time (it is also localised when you send `Accept-Language`).

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "validation_failed",
    "message": "name must not be blank",
    "request_id": "req_7Hk2LmQp9",
    "details": [
      { "field": "name", "issue": "blank" },
      { "field": "slug", "issue": "pattern", "pattern": "^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{1,62}$" }
    ]
  }
}
```

***

## Projects

### The project object

- **`id`** (_string_) — Unique identifier, always prefixed with `prj_`.
- **`name`** (_string_) — Display name, 1–120 characters.
- **`slug`** (_string_) — URL-safe name, unique per workspace. Generated from `name` when omitted.
- **`status`** (_string_) — One of `active`, `paused`, `archived`.
- **`owner`** (_object_) — The user who owns the project.
    - **`id`** (_string_) — User ID, prefixed with `usr_`.
    - **`email`** (_string_) — Primary email address.
    - **`display_name`** (_string \| null_) — `null` for invited users who never signed in.
- **`settings`** (_object_)
    - **`visibility`** (_string_) — `private` (default) or `internal`.
    - **`default_branch`** (_string_) — Defaults to `main`.
    - **`notifications`** (_object_)
        - **`email`** (_boolean_) — Send email digests to members.
        - **`slack_channel`** (_string \| null_) — e.g. `#proj-website`.
- **`created_at`**, **`updated_at`** (_string, RFC 3339_)
- **`archived_at`** (_string \| null_) — Set when `status` becomes `archived`.

### GET /v1/projects

Lists the projects the token can see, newest first.   

| Parameter | In | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `limit` | query | integer | no | 1–100, default `20` |
| `cursor` | query | string | no | Cursor from a previous response |
| `status` |query| string | no | Filter by status; comma-separated for several, e.g. `active,paused`. Archived projects are excluded unless you ask for them explicitly |
| `q` | query | string | no| Case-insensitive substring match on `name` and `slug` |
| `owner_id`| query | string | no | Only projects owned by this user (`usr_...`) |

```bash
curl -sS "https://api.acme.example.com/v1/projects?limit=50&status=active,paused" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACME_TOKEN" \
  -H "Accept: application/json" \
  | jq -r '.data[] | [.id, .name, .status] | @tsv'
```

### GET /v1/projects/{project_id}

Fetches a single project.

Parameter | In | Type | Description
--- | --- | --- | ---
`project_id` | path | string | Project ID (`prj_...`) **or** slug
`expand[]` | query | string | Expand related objects; only `owner` and `members` are supported right now

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
ETag: W/"a3f9"
X-RateLimit-Limit: 600
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 597
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1714555860

{
  "id": "prj_01HV3Q4ZK8",
  "name": "Website relaunch",
  "slug": "website-relaunch",
  "status": "active",
  "owner": { "id": "usr_8812", "email": "lea.moreau@example.com", "display_name": "Léa Moreau" },
  "settings": { "visibility": "private", "default_branch": "main", "notifications": { "email": true, "slack_channel": "#proj-website" } },
  "created_at": "2024-03-11T08:15:22Z",
  "updated_at": "2024-04-30T17:02:09Z",
  "archived_at": null
}
```

### POST /v1/projects

Creates a project. Requires the `projects:write` scope.

| Field | Type | Required | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- |
| `name` | string | ✔ | 1–120 characters |
| `slug` | string |  | Must match `^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{1,62}$`; generated when omitted |
| `visibility` | string |  | `private` \| `internal` |
| `template_id` | string |  | Copy settings and labels from an existing project. Members of the template are **not** copied, which surprises somebody roughly once a week, so we are saying it twice: members are not copied. |

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.acme.example.com/v1/projects \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACME_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: 6c1f0e9a-5b7d-4f43-9b0e-2d1c3a4b5e6f" \
  -d '{
        "name": "Mobile app 2.0",
        "visibility": "internal",
        "template_id": "prj_01HQ9ZT1AA"
      }'
```

Returns `201 Created` with the project object and a `Location` header. Repeating a request with the same `Idempotency-Key` within 24 hours returns the original response instead of creating a duplicate; reusing the key with a *different* body returns `409 Conflict` with code `idempotency_key_reused`.

### PATCH /v1/projects/{project_id}

Partial update: only the fields you send are changed. Send `null` to reset a field to its default (where the field allows it).

```http
PATCH /v1/projects/prj_01HV3Q4ZK8 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.acme.example.com
Authorization: Bearer acme_pat_2f9c1d7e8b4a40c6a1d3e5f7
Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json
If-Match: W/"a3f9"

{"name": "Website relaunch (2024)", "settings": {"notifications": {"slack_channel": null}}}
```

> **Note**
> `PATCH` honours `If-Match`. When the ETag no longer matches you get `412 Precondition Failed`
and nothing is written. The official SDKs re-fetch and retry once on their own.

### DELETE /v1/projects/{project_id} ###

Archives the project (soft delete). Archived projects are read-only and are purged after 30 days; until then `POST /v1/projects/{project_id}/restore` brings them back.

Returns `204 No Content`.



## Members

### GET /v1/projects/{project_id}/members

| Parameter | In | Type | Description |
|-----------|----|------|-------------|
| `project_id` | path | string | Project ID or slug |
| `role` | query | string | `owner`, `maintainer`, `developer` or `viewer` |
| `limit`, `cursor` | query | | See [Pagination](#pagination) |

### POST /v1/projects/{project_id}/members

Invites a user by email address. If the person doesn't have an Acme account yet they receive an invitation email, and the membership has `"state": "pending"` until they accept; invitations expire after 7 days. You can invite at most 50 people per project per hour — exceeding that returns `429` with code `invite_rate_limited`. This limit is separate from the general rate limit and is *not* reflected in the `X-RateLimit-*` headers, which, yes, we know is confusing (see [#1874](https://github.com/acme/projects-api/issues/1874)).

```json
{ "email": "j.tanaka@example.com", "role": "developer", "message": "ようこそ！ Welcome to the team 🎉" }
```

### DELETE /v1/projects/{project_id}/members/{user_id}

Removes a member. The last `owner` of a project can't be removed (`409`, code `last_owner`); transfer ownership first.

## Webhooks <sup>beta</sup>

Deliveries are `POST` requests with a JSON body and an `Acme-Signature` header that looks like `t=1714555860,v1=5257a869e7ecebeda32affa62cdca3fa51cad7e77a0e56ff536d0ce8e108d8bd`. Respond with any `2xx` within 10 seconds, otherwise the delivery is retried with exponential back-off (1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, 12 h — five attempts in total).

Events
:   `project.created`, `project.updated`, `project.archived`, `project.restored`
:   `member.invited`, `member.joined`, `member.removed`

To verify a delivery:

1. Take the raw request body — the bytes, *before* any JSON parsing.
2. Compute an HMAC-SHA256 over `"{t}.{raw_body}"` with your endpoint secret:

   ```python
   import hashlib, hmac

   signed = f"{t}.".encode() + raw_body
   expected = hmac.new(secret.encode(), signed, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
   ```

3. Compare with the `v1=` value using a constant-time comparison:

   ```python
   ok = hmac.compare_digest(expected, received_v1)
   ```
4. Reject deliveries whose `t` is more than five minutes old, to prevent replays.

## Status codes

| Code | Meaning | Typical `error.code` values |
|----:|:----------|:--------------|
| 200 | OK | — |
| 201 | Created | — |
| 204 | No Content | — |
| 400 | Bad Request | `invalid_json`, `invalid_parameter` |
| 401 | Unauthorized | `token_missing`, `token_invalid` |
| 403 | Forbidden | `insufficient_scope` |
| 404 | Not Found | `project_not_found`, `member_not_found` |
| 409 | Conflict | `slug_taken`, `idempotency_key_reused`, `last_owner` |
| 410 | Gone | `cursor_expired` |
| 412 | Precondition Failed | `etag_mismatch` |
| 422 | Unprocessable Entity | `validation_failed` |
| 429 | Too Many Requests | `rate_limited`, `invite_rate_limited` |
| 500 | Internal Server Error | `internal` — include the `request_id` when you contact support |
| 503 | Service Unavailable | `maintenance`; check the [status] page |

- - -

#### Changes to this page

* **2024-05-02** — documented `expand[]`; fixed the default for `limit` (it was never 25).
* **2024-03-18** — added `Idempotency-Key` and the webhook signature scheme.
* **2024-01-09** — first version.

Questions? Open an issue on GitHub (https://github.com/acme/projects-api/issues),\
or write to [api-support@acme.example.com](mailto:api-support@acme.example.com).

[versioning]: https://docs.acme.example.com/policies/versioning "API versioning and deprecation policy"
[status]: https://status.acme.example.com

# API reference: `acme_client`

[![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/acme-client.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/acme-client/)
[![Python versions](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/acme-client.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/acme-client/)
[![Docs](https://readthedocs.org/projects/acme-client/badge/?version=stable)](https://acme-client.readthedocs.io/en/stable/?badge=stable)
[![Typed](https://img.shields.io/badge/typing-PEP%20561-informational)](https://peps.python.org/pep-0561/)

This page documents the public API of `acme_client` **3.x**. Anything not listed here — every name that starts with an underscore, and the whole `acme_client._internal` package — is private and may change in a patch release. Type hints in the signatures are the source of truth: if this page and the hints disagree, the hints win and this page has a bug, so please [tell us](https://github.com/acme/acme-client-python/issues/new?template=docs.yml&labels=docs,good+first+issue&title=%5Bdocs%5D+) about it.

Module overview
---------------

| Name | Kind | Summary |
|:-----|:----:|:--------|
| [`Client`][acme_client.Client] | class | Synchronous client, thread-safe |
| [`AsyncClient`][acme_client.AsyncClient] | class | `asyncio` client with the same surface |
| [`paginate()`][acme_client.paginate] | function | Iterate over every item of a list endpoint |
| [`configure_logging()`][acme_client.configure_logging] | function | Opinionated logging setup for scripts and notebooks |
| `acme_client.errors` | module | Exception hierarchy, see [Exceptions](#exceptions) |
| `acme_client.types` | module | `TypedDict`s and enums for request/response payloads |

Install with `pip install acme-client`, or `pip install "acme-client[http2]"` to get HTTP/2 through `h2`.

## Client

```python
class acme_client.Client(
    token: str | None = None,
    *,
    base_url: str = "https://api.acme.example.com",
    timeout: float | httpx.Timeout | None = 10.0,
    max_retries: int = 3,
    user_agent: str | None = None,
    transport: httpx.BaseTransport | None = None,
    **httpx_kwargs: Any,
)
```

The main entry point. A `Client` owns a connection pool, so create one and reuse it.
Creating a client per request works, but it is slow and will eventually exhaust file
descriptors on a busy worker.[^threads]

**Parameters**

- **token** (*str \| None*) – API token. When omitted it is read from the `ACME_TOKEN`
  environment variable; if that is unset as well, [`ConfigurationError`](#exceptions) is raised.
- **base_url** (*str*) – Override for self-managed installations, e.g. `https://acme.internal.example.net`.
- **timeout** (*float \| httpx.Timeout \| None*) – Seconds, or a full `httpx.Timeout`. `None` disables timeouts completely, which you almost never want.
- **max_retries** (*int*) – Retries for idempotent requests on connection errors, `429` and `5xx` responses. Back-off is exponential with full jitter, capped at 30 s. Set max_retries to 0 to turn retries off.
- **user_agent** (*str \| None*) – Appended to the default `acme-client/3.x python/3.y` string.
- **transport** (*httpx.BaseTransport \| None*) – Custom transport; mostly useful in tests together with `httpx.MockTransport`.
- **\*\*httpx_kwargs** – Any other keyword arguments are passed straight to `httpx.Client` (for example `proxies` or `verify`).

**Raises**

- **ConfigurationError** – no token could be found, or `base_url` is not an absolute `https://` URL.

!!! tip "Use it as a context manager"
    `Client` supports `with Client() as client: ...`, which closes the pool deterministically.
    Long-running services can call [`client.close()`][acme_client.Client.close] on shutdown instead.

#### `Client.fetch(url, *, timeout=None)`

Low-level escape hatch: performs an authenticated `GET` against any path and returns the decoded JSON body.

```python
def fetch(self, url: str, *, timeout: float | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]: ...
```

Parameters
:   **url** (*str*) – Absolute URL, or a path relative to `base_url` such as `/v1/projects`.
:   **timeout** (*float \| None*) – Per-call override of the client timeout.

Returns
:   *dict[str, Any]* – the decoded JSON body.

Raises
:   [`NotFound`][acme_client.errors.NotFound] – the resource doesn't exist.
:   [`RateLimited`][acme_client.errors.RateLimited] – retries were exhausted.

#### `Client.projects.list(*, status=None, q=None, limit=20)`

Returns the first page of projects as a [`Page`][acme_client.Page]. A `Page` is iterable and has
`.has_more` and `.next_cursor`; use [`paginate()`](#paginate) when you want every item. Note that
`len(page)` is the size of *this* page only — the dunder \_\_len\_\_ never triggers a request.

```pycon
>>> from acme_client import Client
>>> client = Client(token="acme_pat_test")
>>> page = client.projects.list(status="active", limit=2)
>>> [p.name for p in page]
['Website relaunch', 'Mobile app 2.0']
>>> page.has_more
True
>>> page.next_cursor  # opaque, don't parse it
'eyJpZCI6InByal8wMUhROVpUMUFBIn0='
```

- **status** (*str \| Sequence[str] \| None*) – `"active"`, `"paused"`, `"archived"`, or several of them.
- **q** (*str \| None*) – Case-insensitive substring filter on name and slug.
- **limit** (*int*) – Page size, 1–100.

#### `Client.projects.create(name, *, slug=None, visibility="private", template_id=None, idempotency_key=None)`

Creates a project and returns a [`Project`][acme_client.types.Project].
If `idempotency_key` is not given, one is generated automatically (a UUID4) so that the built-in
retries are safe. Pass your own key if you retry at a higher level, e.g. from a task queue.

#### `Client.get_project(project_id)`

!!! warning "Deprecated since 2.3"
    Use [`client.projects.get()`][acme_client.resources.Projects.get] instead. `get_project()` will be
    removed in **4.0**. It emits a `DeprecationWarning` on every call, which Python hides by default
    unless you run with `-W default` or under pytest.

```python
# before
project = client.get_project("prj_01HV3Q4ZK8")
# after
project = client.projects.get("prj_01HV3Q4ZK8")
```

***

## AsyncClient

```python
class acme_client.AsyncClient(token: str | None = None, *, base_url: str = ..., timeout: float | httpx.Timeout | None = 10.0, max_retries: int = 3, **httpx_kwargs: Any)
```

Same parameters and the same resource namespaces as [`Client`][acme_client.Client], but every
method is a coroutine. Close it with `await client.aclose()`, or use `async with`.

```python
import asyncio
from acme_client import AsyncClient

async def main() -> None:
    async with AsyncClient() as client:
        a, b = await asyncio.gather(
            client.projects.get("website-relaunch"),
            client.projects.get("mobile-app-2-0"),
        )
        print(a.status, b.status)

asyncio.run(main())
```


## Functions

### paginate

```python
def paginate(fn: Callable[..., Page[T]], /, *args: Any, page_size: int = 100, **kwargs: Any) -> Iterator[T]
```

Calls *fn* repeatedly, following `next_cursor`, and yields every item. Extra positional
arguments (\*args) and keyword arguments (\*\*kwargs) are passed to *fn* unchanged on every call — except `cursor` and `limit`, which `paginate` manages itself and will overwrite (a warning is logged if you pass them anyway).

```pycon
>>> from acme_client import paginate
>>> names = [p.name for p in paginate(client.projects.list, status="active")]
>>> len(names)
137
```

There is also `apaginate()` for [`AsyncClient`][acme_client.AsyncClient], which returns an async iterator; use it with `async for`.

### configure_logging

```python
def configure_logging(level: int | str = "INFO", *, json: bool = False, redact: bool = True) -> None
```

- **level** – passed to `logging.basicConfig`.
- **json** (*bool*) – emit one JSON object per line (handy in containers).
- **redact** (*bool*) – mask tokens and `Authorization` headers. Turning this off is only meant for local debugging; _never_ ship it.

## Exceptions

All exceptions live in `acme_client.errors` and are re-exported from the package root.

    AcmeError
     ├── ConfigurationError
     └── APIError
          ├── BadRequest           (400)
          ├── AuthenticationError  (401)
          ├── PermissionDenied     (403)
          ├── NotFound             (404)
          ├── Conflict             (409)
          ├── RateLimited          (429)
          └── ServerError          (5xx)

| Exception | HTTP status | Useful attributes | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| `AcmeError` | — | | Base class; catch this if you don't care about the details |
| `ConfigurationError` | — | | Raised at construction time, never during a request |
| `APIError` | any | `.status`, `.code`, `.message`, `.request_id` | Always include `request_id` in support tickets |
| `PermissionDenied` | 403 | `.required_scope` | e.g. `"projects:write"` |
| `Conflict` | 409 | `.code` | `slug_taken`, `idempotency_key_reused`, `last_owner` |
| `RateLimited` | 429 | `.retry_after` (*float*, seconds) | Only raised once `max_retries` is exhausted |
| `ServerError` | 500–599 | | Retried automatically for idempotent requests |

```python
import time

from acme_client import Client
from acme_client.errors import Conflict, RateLimited

client = Client()
try:
    client.projects.create("Website relaunch", slug="website-relaunch")
except Conflict as exc:
    if exc.code != "slug_taken":
        raise
except RateLimited as exc:
    time.sleep(exc.retry_after)
```

## Types
`acme_client.types` contains plain `TypedDict`s (for payloads you build) and frozen dataclasses (for objects the API returns). The dataclasses accept unknown fields and keep them in `.extra`, so a newer server never breaks an older client — this is deliberate, please don't "fix" it.[^compat]

Project
:   `id`, `name`, `slug`, `status` (`ProjectStatus`), `owner` (`User`), `settings`, `created_at`, `updated_at`, `archived_at`

User
:   `id`, `email`, `display_name`

ProjectStatus
:   `ACTIVE`, `PAUSED`, `ARCHIVED` — a `str` enum, so `ProjectStatus.ACTIVE == "active"` is `True`.

[^threads]: `Client` is thread-safe. `AsyncClient` is **not** safe to share between event loops.

[^compat]: The policy is written down in `CONTRIBUTING.md` under *Forward compatibility*.

    In short: the client must never raise because the server sent a field it doesn't know about,
    and enums fall back to a plain `str` for values added after the client was released.

# acmectl CLI reference #

[![Latest release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/acme/acmectl?sort=semver&display_name=tag)](https://github.com/acme/acmectl/releases/latest) [![Homebrew](https://img.shields.io/homebrew/v/acmectl)](https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/acmectl) [![Scoop](https://img.shields.io/scoop/v/acmectl?bucket=extras)](https://scoop.sh/#/apps?q=acmectl&s=0&d=1&o=true)

`acmectl` is the command-line client for the Acme platform. This page is the complete
reference for **acmectl 3.4**. The same text is available offline via
`acmectl help <command>`, and as `man acmectl-<command>` if you installed the
Homebrew or `.deb` package.

## Synopsis

```text
acmectl [global flags] <command> [<subcommand>] [flags] [args...]
```

Commands at a glance:

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| [`login`](#acmectl-login) / `logout` | Authenticate against an Acme host |
| [`deploy`](#acmectl-deploy) | Roll out a new revision of a service |
| [`logs`](#acmectl-logs) | Stream or search service logs |
| [`projects`](#acmectl-projects) | List, create and archive projects |
| [`config`](#acmectl-config) | Read and write CLI configuration |
| [`completion`](#shell-completion) | Generate shell completion scripts |

## Global flags
Global flags are accepted by every command. They _should_ come before the command name (`acmectl -o json projects list`); putting them after the command works for most commands, but not all of them.[^order]

`-c`, `--config <path>`
:   Path to the config file. Default: `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/acme/config.toml`, falling back to `~/.config/acme/config.toml` (or `%APPDATA%\acme\config.toml` on Windows).

`-p`, `--profile <name>`
:   Profile from the config file to use. Overrides `ACME_PROFILE`.

`-o`, `--output <format>`
:   One of `table` (the default when stdout is a terminal), `json` (the default otherwise), `yaml`, `jsonl`, `name`, or `template=<go template>`. With `template=` you get the full Go `text/template` language plus the [Sprig](https://masterminds.github.io/sprig/) function library, e.g. `-o 'template={{range .}}{{.id}}{{"\t"}}{{.name | upper}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}'`, which is powerful, occasionally baffling, and the main reason the much simpler `name` format exists at all — if all you need is IDs for a shell loop, use `-o name`.

`-v`, `--verbose`
:   Increase log verbosity. Repeat it for more: `-vv` logs every HTTP request, `-vvv` also logs bodies (with tokens redacted).

`-q`, `--quiet`
:   Only print errors.

`--no-color`
:   Disable ANSI colours. `NO_COLOR=1` is honoured too.

`--timeout <duration>`
:   Network timeout such as `30s` or `2m`. Default: `60s`.

## acmectl login

```text
acmectl login [--token-stdin] [--sso] [--host <url>]
```

| Flag | Default | Description |
|:-----|:-------:|:------------|
| `--token-stdin` | `false` | Read a personal access token from stdin instead of opening a browser |
| `--sso` | `false` | Use the SSO device-code flow |
| `--host` | `https://api.acme.example.com` | API host, for self-managed installations |

1. Interactive login (opens your browser):

   ```console
   $ acmectl login
   ! First copy your one-time code: 4F2A-9C1B
   Press Enter to open acme.example.com in your browser...
   ✓ Logged in as lea.moreau (profile "default")
   ```

2. In CI, with the token stored as a secret:

   ```bash
   echo "$ACME_TOKEN" | acmectl login --token-stdin --host https://acme.corp.example.net
   ```

`acmectl logout` removes the stored credentials for the current profile. Add `--all` to remove every profile's credentials.

## acmectl deploy

```text
acmectl deploy [flags] <service> [<image>]
acmectl deploy status <service>
acmectl deploy promote <service>
acmectl deploy rollback <service> [--to <revision>]
```

Deploys a new revision of `<service>`. When `<image>` is omitted the image of the current revision is reused, which is handy for config-only changes. The command waits until the rollout is healthy (or `--timeout` passes) and streams events in the meantime; press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> to stop watching — the rollout itself carries on in the background, and `acmectl deploy status <service>` picks it up again.

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--env` | `-e` | string | `staging` | Target environment |
| `--set` | | `key=value`, repeatable | | Override a config value; nested keys use dots, e.g. `--set 'db.pool.max=20'` |
| `--set-file` | | `key=path` | | Like `--set`, but reads the value from a file |
| `--strategy` | | `rolling\|blue-green\|canary` | `rolling` | Rollout strategy |
| `--canary-weight` | | int | `10` | Percentage of traffic sent to the canary |
| `--wait` | | bool | `true` | Wait for the rollout to finish |
| `--dry-run` | | `none\|client\|server` | `none` | Validate without applying anything |

Examples:

1. Deploy a specific image to production:

   ```bash
   acmectl deploy -e production checkout ghcr.io/acme/checkout:1.42.0
   ```

2. Canary with 5% of the traffic, then promote it:

   ```bash
   acmectl deploy checkout --strategy canary --canary-weight 5
   acmectl deploy promote checkout
   ```

3. Change a setting without building a new image:

   ```bash
   acmectl deploy checkout \
     --set 'feature_flags.new_cart=true' \
     --set-file 'tls.cert=./certs/checkout.pem'
   ```

## acmectl logs

```text
acmectl logs <service> [-f] [--since <duration>] [--grep <regex>] [--instance <id>]
```

`-f`, `--follow`
:   Keep streaming new lines until interrupted.

`--since <duration>`
:   Only show lines newer than this (`10m`, `2h`, `1d`). Default: `15m`.

`--grep <regex>`
:   RE2 syntax. Case-sensitive unless you prefix the pattern with `(?i)`.

`--instance <id>`
:   Only one instance; get the IDs from `acmectl deploy status`.

## acmectl projects

```text
acmectl projects list    [--status active|paused|archived] [--limit N]
acmectl projects create  <name> [--visibility private|internal]
acmectl projects archive <project>
```

Here `|` means "one of" — it's not a shell pipe :)

## acmectl config

`acmectl config get <key>`, `acmectl config set <key> <value>` and `acmectl config list`. Keys use dots (`defaults.env`, `output.color`). Unknown keys are rejected unless you pass `--force`, so that typos don't silently create settings that do nothing.

## Shell completion

=== "bash"

    ```bash
    acmectl completion bash | sudo tee /etc/bash_completion.d/acmectl > /dev/null
    ```

=== "zsh"

    ```zsh
    acmectl completion zsh > "${fpath[1]}/_acmectl"
    autoload -U compinit && compinit
    ```

=== "fish"

    ```fish
    acmectl completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/acmectl.fish
    ```

=== "PowerShell"

    ```powershell
    acmectl completion powershell | Out-String | Invoke-Expression
    ```

Restart your shell afterwards.[^completion]

## Environment variables

| Variable | Equivalent flag | Notes |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `ACME_TOKEN` | — | Takes precedence over stored credentials; handy in CI |
| `ACME_HOST` | `--host` | |
| `ACME_PROFILE` | `--profile` | |
| `ACME_OUTPUT` | `--output` | |
| `ACME_CONFIG` | `--config` | |
| `NO_COLOR` | `--no-color` | Any non-empty value |
| `HTTPS_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY` | | Standard proxy variables, see <https://pkg.go.dev/net/http#ProxyFromEnvironment> |

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|-----:|:--------|
| 0 | Success |
| 1 | Generic error |
| 2 | Invalid usage (unknown flag, missing argument) |
| 3 | Not authenticated, or the token expired |
| 4 | Resource not found |
| 5 | Conflict, e.g. a deployment is already in progress |
| 10 | Rollout failed its health checks and was rolled back |
| 124 | Timed out waiting (see `--timeout`) |
| 130 | Interrupted with <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> |

[^order]: Since 3.2, `deploy`, `logs` and `projects` accept global flags anywhere on the line; `config` and `completion` still don't, because their arguments are passed through verbatim.
[^completion]: The system bash 3.2 on macOS is not supported. Install bash 5 with Homebrew (`brew install bash bash-completion@2`).

Migrating from v2 to v3 ======================= > **Warning** > v3 drops support for Node.js 16 and removes the CommonJS build. If you can't move to ESM yet, stay on 2.x — it receives security fixes until **30 June 2025**. This guide covers upgrading `@acme/forms` (and `@acme/forms-react`) from 2.x to 3.0. Most apps need about an hour. Apps that use custom validators, the `withForm()` higher-order component, or that reach into `form.errors` directly will need longer; budget half a day and read [Validation results](#validation-results) carefully. If something in here is wrong or unclear, please start a [discussion][discussions] rather than opening an issue — we fold the answers back into this page. Summary of breaking changes --------------------------- | Area | v2 | v3 | Codemod | |:-----|:---|:---|:-------:| | Entry point | `require("@acme/forms")` | `import { createForm } from "@acme/forms"` | ✅ | | Form factory | ~~`new Form(schema, opts)`~~ | `createForm({ schema, ...opts })` | ✅ | | Validators | `(value) => string \| undefined` | `(value) => ValidationResult` | ⚠️ partial | | React binding | ~~`withForm(Component)`~~ | `useForm()` hook | ❌ | | Change events | `onChange(value, field)` | `onChange({ value, field, form })` | ✅ | | Errors | `form.errors` (plain object) | `form.errors` (`Map`) | ❌ | | Async validation | `validateAsync: true` | always on; tune it with `debounceMs` | ✅ | | Node.js | ≥ 16 | ≥ 18.18 | — | | TypeScript | ≥ 4.7 | ≥ 5.2 (we rely on `const` type parameters) | — | Step by step ------------ 1. **Update the packages** and their peers: ```bash npm install @acme/forms@^3 @acme/forms-react@^3 ``` - With pnpm and `strict-peer-dependencies=true`, bump `react` to 18.2+ first. - Yarn PnP users: run `yarn dlx @yarnpkg/sdks vscode` afterwards, or your editor keeps showing the v2 types. * VS Code may additionally need *TypeScript: Restart TS Server*. 2. **Run the codemod.** It takes care of the mechanical renames: ```bash npx @acme/forms-codemod v2-to-v3 "src/**/*.{ts,tsx,js,jsx}" --dry-run --print npx @acme/forms-codemod v2-to-v3 "src/**/*.{ts,tsx,js,jsx}" ``` At the end it prints the files it could **not** fully transform, and it inserts a `// TODO(forms-v3):` comment at each spot that needs a human. Keep that list; steps 4 and 5 deal with it. 3. **Switch your package to ESM.** In `package.json`: ```diff { "name": "my-app", - "main": "dist/index.cjs", + "type": "module", + "exports": "./dist/index.js", "dependencies": { - "@acme/forms": "^2.9.4", + "@acme/forms": "^3.0.0", "react": "^18.2.0" } } ``` Jest users also need to adjust `transformIgnorePatterns`, or switch to Vitest (which we recommend anyway). 4. **Replace `withForm()`** with `useForm()`. The HOC is gone and there is no compatibility shim:
v2 v3
```tsx class Signup extends React.Component { render() { const { form } = this.props; return ; } } export default withForm(Signup, { schema }); ``` ```tsx export default function Signup() { const form = useForm({ schema }); return ; } ```
5. **Update custom validators**, see below. 6. Run your test suite, then click through every form the codemod flagged. ### Validation results In v2 a validator returned an error *string* or `undefined`. In v3 it returns a `ValidationResult`, which can carry several messages, a severity and i18n parameters: ```diff -const noAdmin = (value: string) => - value.toLowerCase() === "admin" ? "This username is reserved" : undefined; +const noAdmin: Validator = (value) => + value.toLowerCase() === "admin" + ? { ok: false, issues: [{ code: "reserved", message: "This username is reserved", severity: "error" }] } + : { ok: true }; ``` The codemod wraps simple string-returning validators in `fromLegacy()`. That works, but it allocates on every keystroke, so replace the wrappers when you get the chance — at least in big forms. > [!WARNING] > `form.errors` is now a `Map`. Code like `form.errors.email` silently returns `undefined` instead > of throwing, so TypeScript is your friend here; JavaScript projects should grep for > `errors.` and `errors[` before shipping. > > ```ts > // v3 > const emailErrors = form.errors.get("email") ?? []; > ``` Upgrade checklist ----------------- - [x] Node.js 18.18+ in CI and in the production images - [ ] Packages bumped to `^3` - [ ] Codemod applied and the diff reviewed - [ ] all `TODO(forms-v3)` comments resolved - [ ] no `fromLegacy()` left in hot paths - [ ] Package switched to ESM - [ ] Jest/Vitest config updated - [ ] Storybook builder updated (`@storybook/react-vite`) - [ ] Custom validators return a `ValidationResult` - [ ] E2E tests green on Chrome **and** Safari Deprecation timeline -------------------- | Version | Date | What happens | |--------:|:----:|:-------------| | 2.9.0 | 2024-01-15 | v3 APIs available under `@acme/forms/next`; `withForm()` logs a deprecation warning | | 3.0.0 | 2024-04-02 | v3 released; the CommonJS build and `withForm()` are removed | | 2.9.x | until 2025-06-30 | Security fixes only | | 4.0.0 | ~2025 | `fromLegacy()` removed | FAQ --- **Can I run v2 and v3 side by side?** Yes, with npm aliases (`"forms-v2": "npm:@acme/forms@^2"`), but the two versions don't share context, so a field can't belong to forms from both. It's meant for page-by-page migrations of large apps, not as a permanent setup. **Where did `Form.prototype.submitAsync` go?** `submit()` is always async now and returns a promise. **The codemod crashes on files with decorators.**\ Pass `--parser=babel-ts` (the default is `tsx`). If it still fails, please attach the file to [#2107](https://github.com/acme/forms/issues/2107). **Is there a v2 → v3 guide for the Vue bindings?** Not yet, see [the tracking issue](https://github.com/acme/forms/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3Avue+label%3Av3-migration). ---
title: "Zero-downtime schema migrations: what we learned"
slug: zero-downtime-schema-migrations
date: 2024-04-18T09:00:00+02:00
lastmod: 2024-04-22
author: Marta Kowalczyk
tags: [postgres, migrations, devops]
categories:
  - Engineering
draft: false
cover: { image: /images/blog/zero-downtime/cover.jpg, alt: "A crane lifting a container off a moving freight train" }
summary: How we went from 40-minute maintenance windows to shipping schema changes on a Friday afternoon, and the three outages it took to get there.
---

Two years ago every schema change at Acme came with a calendar invite: “Maintenance window, Sunday 06:00–06:40 CET, expect errors.” We’d put up the status-page banner on Thursday, someone would set three alarms, and on Sunday morning that someone — usually me — would sit in a dark kitchen watching `ALTER TABLE` crawl through 180 million rows while the coffee went cold. Last month we shipped 23 migrations to production, most of them during office hours, and nobody outside the platform team noticed. This post is about how we got there, and about the three outages we caused along the way.

<!--more-->

## Why “just run the migration” stops working

Postgres is remarkably good at a lot of things, but some DDL statements take an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock on the table, and that lock conflicts with *everything*, including plain `SELECT`s. The statement itself is often quick. The problem is the queue: if a long-running query holds even a weak lock on the table, your `ALTER` waits for it, and every query that arrives after your `ALTER` waits behind it. Within a few seconds the connection pool is exhausted, the API starts returning 503s, and the pager goes off for something that “should have taken 20 milliseconds”.

![Diagram: one ALTER TABLE waiting behind a long-running SELECT, with hundreds of queries queued behind it](/images/blog/zero-downtime/lock-queue.png)
*Figure 1: The lock queue. The `ALTER` itself needs 20 ms; the damage comes from everything stuck behind it.*

> “The migration wasn’t slow. The migration was _waiting_ — and everyone else was waiting for the migration.”
>
> — from our incident review, March 2023

## Outage #1: the innocent default

Our first attempt at running migrations during the day went wrong within a week. We added a column with a volatile default to `orders`, our busiest table. On Postgres 11+ a *constant* default is a metadata-only change, but `now()` is not constant, so Postgres had to rewrite the entire table while holding the lock.[^pg11]

```sql
-- looks harmless; rewrites 180M rows under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
ALTER TABLE orders
    ADD COLUMN fulfilled_at timestamptz DEFAULT now();
```

What we do now is boring and safe: add the column without a default, set the default separately (which only affects new rows), and backfill existing rows in small batches from a background job.

```sql
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN fulfilled_at timestamptz;
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN fulfilled_at SET DEFAULT now();

-- backfill, 5 000 rows at a time, from a worker that sleeps between batches
UPDATE orders
   SET fulfilled_at = updated_at
 WHERE id IN (
       SELECT id FROM orders
        WHERE fulfilled_at IS NULL AND status = 'fulfilled'
        LIMIT 5000
        FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
 );
```

## Outage #2: the index that ate the replica

Everybody knows you should use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. What fewer people know — or at least what *we* didn’t know — is that a concurrent index build that fails halfway leaves an `INVALID` index behind, which is still maintained on every write but never used for reads. Ours failed because of a deadlock with a nightly batch job, our migration tool happily reported success (it didn’t check the exit status of that particular statement, for reasons that made sense to someone in 2019), and for nine days we paid the write cost of an index nobody could use. The replica lag alerts that eventually caught it were, in hindsight, the system politely trying to tell us something.

```sql
SELECT indexrelid::regclass AS index, indrelid::regclass AS "table"
  FROM pg_index
 WHERE NOT indisvalid;
```

That query now runs as a post-migration check, and the deploy fails loudly if it returns anything.

## Outage #3: the foreign key

Adding a foreign key takes a `SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE` lock on *both* tables and validates every existing row while holding it. On a 40-million-row table that took long enough to make checkout time out for about four minutes on a Tuesday afternoon, which is the most expensive four minutes of my career so far. The fix is a two-step dance:

```sql
ALTER TABLE line_items
    ADD CONSTRAINT line_items_order_id_fkey
    FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders (id) NOT VALID;   -- fast, brief lock

ALTER TABLE line_items
    VALIDATE CONSTRAINT line_items_order_id_fkey;              -- slow, but only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE
```

![Grafana screenshot: p99 checkout latency spiking to 30 s for four minutes](/images/blog/zero-downtime/fk-outage.png "Tuesday, 14:12–14:16")
*Figure 2: Checkout p99 during the foreign-key incident. We do not talk about Tuesday.*

***

## What we do now

The short version: every migration is reviewed by a linter, runs with a lock timeout, and is split into expand/contract phases that can each be deployed and rolled back independently. The longer version:

- **Always set `lock_timeout`.** Our migration runner sets `SET lock_timeout = '2s'` before every statement and retries up to five times with jitter. A migration that can’t get its lock fails fast instead of taking the site down; we’d rather retry at 3 a.m. than page someone.
- **Expand, migrate, contract.** Renaming a column is three deploys, not one:
    1. add the new column and write to both;
    2. backfill, then switch reads to the new column;
    3. stop writing the old column, and drop it a release later.
- **Lint the SQL, not just the code.** We run [squawk] in CI on every migration file. It catches most of the classics — volatile defaults, non-concurrent indexes, `NOT NULL` without a check constraint — before a human even looks at the PR.
- **Never trust a green checkmark.** Post-migration checks look for invalid indexes, unvalidated constraints and unexpected table rewrites (via `pg_stat_user_tables.n_tup_upd` jumps).
- **Make the slow part a job.** Backfills are background jobs with progress metrics and a kill switch, __never__ part of the migration transaction itself.
- **Practise on production-sized data.** A nightly restore of an anonymised snapshot runs every pending migration and records how long each lock was held.

We also wrote down the rules in a one-page cheat sheet that lives next to the migrations directory. It is the most-viewed page in our internal wiki, which says something about either the cheat sheet or the wiki.

## Tooling

We looked at several options before settling on our current setup. [strong_migrations] was the inspiration for most of our rules, even though we don’t run Rails; [pgroll](https://github.com/xataio/pgroll) is very promising for the expand/contract part, and we’re watching it closely; and the Postgres docs page on [explicit locking][pg-locks] is, honestly, the best fifteen minutes you can spend before writing your next migration. Our own runner is about 600 lines of Go and is not open source yet… mostly because it still contains the word `TODO` 41 times.

| Check | Tool | Blocks merge? |
|:------|:-----|:-------------:|
| Dangerous DDL patterns | squawk | yes |
| Lock duration on snapshot | nightly job | no (alerts) |
| Invalid indexes after deploy | post-deploy hook | yes |
| Unvalidated constraints | post-deploy hook | yes |

## What’s next

We’re not done. Large enum changes still need a maintenance window, and partitioning `events` (2.1 billion rows and counting) is going to be its own blog post — or possibly its own book. If this kind of problem sounds fun to you, we’re [hiring](https://acme.example.com/careers?team=platform&utm_source=blog&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=zero-downtime).

_Thanks to Jonas, Priya and Ana for reviewing drafts of this post, and to everyone who was on call during the incidents above. Sorry about Tuesday._

***

[^pg11]: Since PostgreSQL 11, `ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT <constant>` stores the default in the catalog and doesn’t rewrite the table. Volatile defaults such as `now()`, `random()` or `gen_random_uuid()` still force a full rewrite.

[^tuesday]: For the record, “Tuesday” is now a verb on our team, as in “let’s not Tuesday the database”.

[squawk]: https://squawkhq.com/ "squawk — a linter for Postgres migrations"
[strong_migrations]: https://github.com/ankane/strong_migrations
[pg-locks]: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html#LOCKING-TABLES

# Q3 2024 planning — Platform team

**Date:** Thu 2024-06-27, 14:00–16:10 CEST (ran 40 min over, sorry)  
**Where:** Room "Lovelace" + Zoom (link in the calendar invite)  
**Notes:** @jkowalski (first half), @amina-r (second half)  
**Status:** draft, please correct anything I got wrong directly in this doc

## Attendees

- @mrossi (EM, facilitating)
- @amina-r
- @jkowalski
- @t.nguyen — joined ~14:35
- @sofia.l (PM)
- @dkim (SRE, guest for item 3)
- absent: @pbauer (OOO), @lchen (sick)

## Agenda

1. Q2 retro: what shipped / what didn't (15 min)
2. OKR draft review (30 min)
3. Postgres 16 upgrade — go / no-go
4. On-call load & the pager situation
5. Hiring update
6. AOB

---

## 1. Q2 retro

- shipped
  - multi-region read replicas (finally!!)
  - new deploy pipeline, p50 ~35% faster, p95 basically unchanged
    - p50 win is mostly the docker layer cache, see PLAT-1182
    - p95 is dominated by the integration-test stage, which nobody owns
  - self-serve feature flags v1, adoption 11 teams out of 19
- didn't ship
  - cost dashboards — blocked on the finance data export, *again*
    - finance says end of July; @sofia.l is skeptical
  - k8s 1.29 upgrade, moved to Q3
  - runbook cleanup (nobody picked it up, which tells us something)
- went well: pairing on the replica work, fewer "quick questions" in #platform
  since we started the office hours
- went badly: three P2 incidents caused by config drift between staging & prod,
  two of them on a Friday

> "We keep saying staging is 'basically prod'. It isn't. It's prod's younger
> sibling that never cleans its room." — @t.nguyen

TODO: @jkowalski link the three incident docs here

---

## 2. OKR draft

Draft from @mrossi, discussed line by line. Numbers are the proposed targets, not commitments yet.

Objective | Key result | Baseline | Target | Owner
--- | --- | --- | --- | ---
O1 Reliable deploys | KR1 change failure rate | 14% | < 8% | @amina-r
O1 | KR2 p95 deploy time | 31 min |18 min| @jkowalski
O2 Cheaper infra | KR1 compute spend vs Q2 | 100% | 88% | @t.nguyen
O2 | KR2 % of services with cost labels | 41% | 95% | @sofia.l
O3 Happier on-call | KR1 pages / week (median) | 23 | ≤ 10 | @mrossi
O3 | KR2 runbooks for top-20 alerts | 6 | 20 | ???

Discussion:
- O2/KR1 might be too aggressive; @t.nguyen thinks 92% is realistic w/o
  touching the data platform, 88% only if we also move the batch jobs to spot
  - @dkim: spot for batch is fine, we did it at my last company, but you need
    checkpointing or you'll eat the retries
  - agreed to keep 88% as stretch, 92% as the "committed" number
- O3/KR2 has no owner. Nobody volunteered. Awkward silence. Moving on.
- @sofia.l asked whether "happier on-call" can be measured at all; proposal: add
  a 2-question survey after each rotation. People were lukewarm but nobody objected.

**Decision:** OKRs go to the dept. review on 07-03 with the changes above. O3/KR2
owner to be assigned by @mrossi before then.

---

## 3. Postgres 16 upgrade

@dkim presented the plan (slides in the shared drive, "pg16-upgrade-v3-FINAL-really.pdf").

- approach: logical replication to a new PG16 cluster, then switch over
  - est. downtime: < 60 s for the switchover itself
  - rollback = reverse replication, tested in staging twice
- risks
  - extensions: `pg_partman` needs a version bump first; `timescaledb` not used anymore
    (but the extension is still installed in 2 DBs?? → check)
  - sequences are not replicated by logical replication → must sync manually right
    before the switchover; script exists, see PLAT-1240
  - the analytics team's long-running queries — they need a heads-up 2 weeks in advance
- open question: do we do all 14 clusters in Q3 or just the 4 critical ones?

> @amina-r: "If we only do four we'll be running two major versions for half a
> year, and that's how we ended up on 12 in the first place."
>
> @dkim: "Fair. But four done properly beats fourteen done in a rush."

**Decision:** go for the 4 critical clusters in Q3 (`orders`, `billing`, `identity`, `catalog`),
remaining 10 in Q4. @dkim owns the plan, @amina-r is the platform counterpart.

---

## 4. On-call load

# RFC 0042: Async plugin hooks

- Feature Name: `async_plugins`
- Start Date: 2024-02-12
- RFC PR: [acme/rfcs#42](https://github.com/acme/rfcs/pull/42)
- Tracking Issue: [acme/forge#3817](https://github.com/acme/forge/issues/3817)
- Authors: Priya Raman (@priyar), Jonas Weber (@jweber)
- Status: **Accepted** (FCP ended 2024-03-29)

## Summary

Allow Forge plugins to implement their hooks as `async` functions, both in Rust
and in TypeScript, so that plugins can perform I/O (network requests, reading
large files, talking to a language server) without blocking the build
scheduler. Existing synchronous plugins keep working unchanged.

## Motivation

Today every hook runs on one of the scheduler's worker threads and is expected
to return quickly. In practice, plugins do all sorts of slow things in hooks:

* fetching remote modules (`https://` imports in the `remote-imports` plugin),
* calling out to `esbuild` or `swc` subprocesses,
* querying a database for content (the CMS plugins), and
* waiting for a TypeScript language service to type-check a file.

When a hook blocks, the worker thread is gone for that time. With the default
pool of `num_cpus` workers, four slow fetches on a laptop are enough to stall
the whole build. We have seen this in the wild repeatedly — see [#2950],
[#3101] and the infamous "build hangs on airplane wifi" thread.[^wifi]

Plugin authors currently work around it in one of three ways, all of them bad:

1. **Spawning their own runtime.** Several plugins create a private Tokio
   runtime inside the hook and `block_on` a future:

   ```rust
   fn on_load(&self, ctx: &mut LoadContext) -> Result<Option<Module>> {
       let rt = tokio::runtime::Runtime::new()?; // a new runtime. per call.
       rt.block_on(self.fetch(ctx.url()))
   }
   ```

   This still blocks the worker, creates threads on every call, and panics if
   the hook happens to be invoked from inside an existing runtime.

2. **Pre-fetching everything in `on_start`.** Works for small sites, falls
   over for anything with more than a few hundred remote resources, and makes
   incremental rebuilds pointless.

3. **Giving up**, and telling users to run a separate script before the build.

None of these compose. Two plugins that each spin up a runtime will happily
fight over the same file descriptors, and nobody can reason about the result.

## Guide-level explanation

With this RFC, a Rust plugin can implement hooks as `async fn`:

```rust
use forge_plugin::prelude::*;

pub struct RemoteImports {
    client: reqwest::Client,
}

impl Plugin for RemoteImports {
    async fn on_load(&self, ctx: &mut LoadContext<'_>) -> Result<Option<Module>> {
        if !ctx.url().starts_with("https://") {
            return Ok(None);
        }
        let body = self.client.get(ctx.url()).send().await?.text().await?;
        Ok(Some(Module::js(body)))
    }
}
```

and a TypeScript plugin simply returns a promise:

```ts
import { definePlugin } from "@forge/plugin";

export default definePlugin({
  name: "cms-content",
  async onLoad(ctx) {
    if (!ctx.id.startsWith("cms:")) return null;
    const entry = await cms.getEntry(ctx.id.slice(4));
    return { code: `export default ${JSON.stringify(entry)}`, loader: "js" };
  },
});
```

Nothing else changes for plugin authors. Sync hooks keep working, and a plugin
may mix sync and async hooks freely.

## Reference-level explanation

### Hook signatures

All hook methods on the `Plugin` trait become `async fn`s, using native
async-fn-in-trait (stable since Rust 1.75, which is already our MSRV). A
blanket adapter, `SyncPlugin`, keeps the old signatures compiling:

```rust
pub trait Plugin: Send + Sync + 'static {
    async fn on_start(&self, _ctx: &mut StartContext<'_>) -> Result<()> { Ok(()) }
    async fn on_resolve(&self, _ctx: &mut ResolveContext<'_>) -> Result<Option<Resolved>> { Ok(None) }
    async fn on_load(&self, _ctx: &mut LoadContext<'_>) -> Result<Option<Module>> { Ok(None) }
    async fn on_end(&self, _ctx: &mut EndContext<'_>) -> Result<()> { Ok(()) }
}
```

### Scheduling

1. The scheduler moves from a fixed thread pool to a multi-threaded Tokio
   runtime.

   Sync hooks are run through `spawn_blocking`, so a slow sync hook occupies a
   blocking thread rather than a core worker. The blocking pool is capped at
   `max(64, 4 * num_cpus)` threads; the cap is configurable as
   `scheduler.blocking_threads`.

2. Async hooks are polled on the core workers.

   A hook that blocks *inside* an `async fn` (e.g. `std::fs::read` on a slow
   network drive) will still stall a worker. In debug builds we detect polls
   that take longer than 50 ms and log a warning that names the plugin and
   the hook.

3. Hook ordering is unchanged: for each module, `on_resolve` hooks run in
   plugin order until one returns `Some`, then `on_load` hooks do the same.

   Different modules are processed concurrently, as they are today.

### Cancellation

When a build is cancelled (a file changes during `forge dev`, or the user presses <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd>), outstanding hook
futures are dropped. Plugins must therefore be cancel-safe at every `.await` point. This is the single biggest
behavioural change in this RFC, and it gets its own section in the plugin author guide.

### TypeScript plugins

The JS host already runs an event loop, but today it blocks on each promise
before returning to Rust. After this change promises are bridged to Rust
futures via `forge_js::PromiseFuture`, so up to `js.max_inflight` (default: 32)
hook calls can be pending per isolate.

## Drawbacks

- A more complex scheduler, which is harder to debug.
    - Stack traces through async code are worse, particularly across the JS bridge.
    - `tokio-console` support helps, but it is opt-in.
- Cancel-safety is a new obligation for plugin authors, and getting it wrong
  produces bugs that are rare and hard to reproduce.
- Compile times for `forge-core` grow by roughly 8% (measured on CI, see the
  [benchmark gist](https://gist.github.com/priyar/4b1f0c2d7e9a8b3c5d6e7f8091a2b3c4#file-compile-times-md)).

## Rationale and alternatives

| Option | Pros | Cons | Verdict |
|:-------|:-----|:-----|:-------:|
| **A. Native async hooks** (this RFC) | No workarounds needed; same model for Rust and TS | Scheduler rewrite; cancel-safety | ✅ |
| B. Bigger thread pool | Trivial to implement | Doesn't fix the problem, only moves the cliff | ❌ |
| C. `#[async_trait]` macro | Works on older compilers | Boxes every future, worse error messages, and our MSRV is 1.75 anyway | ❌ |
| D. Callback / continuation API | No async runtime in core | Awful ergonomics (see Prior art) | ❌ |
| E. Separate "fetch" phase before the build | Simple mental model | Breaks incremental builds; doesn't help the LSP use case | ❌ |

We considered shipping B as a stop-gap. It was rejected in the design meeting
on 2024-02-28 because it would make the migration *look* less urgent without
actually fixing anything.

## Prior art

* Rollup and Vite: plugin hooks may return promises, and hooks for different
  modules run concurrently. This RFC is heavily inspired by that model.
* esbuild: `onLoad`/`onResolve` callbacks in JS are async; Go plugins are
  synchronous but run on goroutines, so blocking is cheap.
* Parcel 2: plugins are async throughout and run in worker farms.
* Bazel: no in-process plugins at all; everything is a separate action, which
  sidesteps the problem at a large cost in flexibility.

## Unresolved questions

1. Should `on_end` hooks be allowed to run concurrently with each other? Some
   plugins (`sitemap`, `rss`) write files that others (`compress`) read.
2. What is the right default for `js.max_inflight`? 32 is an educated guess.
3. Do we expose the Tokio runtime handle to plugins, or only a narrow
   `forge_plugin::spawn` API? The latter keeps our options open if we ever
   want to swap the runtime.

## Future possibilities

- Streaming `on_load` results, so that large generated modules don't have to be
  buffered in memory.
- A `Plugin::on_watch` hook for plugins that watch external resources (e.g. a
  CMS webhook) and want to trigger rebuilds.
- Reusing the same machinery for the dev server's HMR pipeline.

[^wifi]: [acme/forge discussion #2777](https://github.com/acme/forge/discussions/2777): a 40-minute
    build that turned out to be one plugin retrying DNS lookups with a 30-second timeout, one after another.

[#2950]: https://github.com/acme/forge/issues/2950
[#3101]: https://github.com/acme/forge/issues/3101 "Build stalls when the remote-imports plugin is enabled"

# Tutorial: deploy the Acme sample shop to Kubernetes

![Architecture of the sample shop: browser, ingress, frontend, API, PostgreSQL](./images/k8s-tutorial/architecture.png "Sample shop architecture")

In this tutorial you'll deploy the **Acme sample shop** — a small three-tier app — to a
local Kubernetes cluster created with [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/), expose it through an
ingress controller, and roll out a new version without downtime. Budget about 45 minutes.

> [!NOTE]
> Everything here runs on your laptop. Nothing is deployed to a cloud account, and you can delete
> all of it in the [Cleanup](#cleanup) step.

## Prerequisites

- [ ] Docker 24+ (or Podman 4.7+ with the Docker-compatible socket enabled)
- [ ] `kind` 0.22+
- [ ] `kubectl` 1.29+
- [ ] `helm` 3.14+ — only for the optional monitoring step
- [x] About 4 GB of free RAM

Check your versions:

```bash
docker version --format '{{.Server.Version}}'
kind version
kubectl version --client
```

## Step 1: Create the cluster

1. Save the following cluster config as `kind-config.yaml`. It maps ports 80 and 443 on your
   machine into the cluster, so the ingress controller is reachable on `localhost`:

   ```yaml
   kind: Cluster
   apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
   name: shop
   nodes:
     - role: control-plane
       kubeadmConfigPatches:
         - |
           kind: InitConfiguration
           nodeRegistration:
             kubeletExtraArgs:
               node-labels: "ingress-ready=true"
       extraPortMappings:
         - containerPort: 80
           hostPort: 80
         - containerPort: 443
           hostPort: 443
     - role: worker
     - role: worker
   ```

2. Create the cluster:

   ```bash
   kind create cluster --config kind-config.yaml
   ```

   Expected output (abridged):

   ```text
   Creating cluster "shop" ...
    ✓ Ensuring node image (kindest/node:v1.29.2)
    ✓ Preparing nodes
    ✓ Writing configuration
    ✓ Starting control-plane
    ✓ Installing CNI
    ✓ Installing StorageClass
    ✓ Joining worker nodes
   Set kubectl context to "kind-shop"
   ```

3. Verify that all three nodes are `Ready`:

   ```bash
   kubectl get nodes
   ```

> [!TIP]
> If `kind create cluster` hangs at *Starting control-plane*, Docker Desktop probably has less
> than 4 GB of memory assigned. Raise it under **Settings → Resources** and try again.

## Step 2: Install the ingress controller

1. Apply the ingress-nginx manifest that is built for kind:

   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/controller-v1.10.0/deploy/static/provider/kind/deploy.yaml
   ```

1. Wait until the controller is ready:

   ```bash
   kubectl wait --namespace ingress-nginx \
     --for=condition=ready pod \
     --selector=app.kubernetes.io/component=controller \
     --timeout=120s
   ```

1. That's it. (Yes, every item above is numbered `1.` — Markdown renumbers them for you.)

## Step 3: Deploy the database

1. Create a namespace and the database credentials:

   ```bash
   kubectl create namespace shop
   kubectl -n shop create secret generic db-credentials \
     --from-literal=POSTGRES_USER=shop \
     --from-literal=POSTGRES_PASSWORD="$(openssl rand -hex 16)"
   ```

2. Apply the PostgreSQL manifest from the repository:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n shop apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/acme/sample-shop/v2.3.0/deploy/k8s/postgres.yaml
   ```

3. Wait for the pod; the first start takes a while because the volume is initialised:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n shop rollout status statefulset/postgres --timeout=180s
   ```

## Step 4: Deploy the API and the frontend

Continuing the numbering from the previous step:

4. Deploy the API. Save this as `api.yaml`:

   ```yaml
   apiVersion: apps/v1
   kind: Deployment
   metadata:
     name: api
     namespace: shop
   spec:
     replicas: 2
     selector:
       matchLabels: { app: api }
     template:
       metadata:
         labels: { app: api }
       spec:
         containers:
           - name: api
             image: ghcr.io/acme/sample-shop-api:2.3.0
             ports:
               - containerPort: 8080
             envFrom:
               - secretRef:
                   name: db-credentials
             readinessProbe:
               httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
               periodSeconds: 5
   ```

   and apply it with `kubectl apply -f api.yaml`.

5. Deploy the frontend, the two services and the ingress in one go:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n shop apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/acme/sample-shop/v2.3.0/deploy/k8s/frontend.yaml
   ```

6. Open <http://shop.localtest.me> in your browser. `localtest.me` resolves to `127.0.0.1`, so no
   `/etc/hosts` editing is needed.

![The sample shop's home page showing three products](./images/k8s-tutorial/shop-home.png)

> [!NOTE]
> On Apple Silicon, kind runs `arm64` nodes. The sample images are multi-arch, but if you build
> your own images you need to build for the right platform and load them into the cluster:
>
> ```bash
> docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64 -t shop-api:dev ./api
> kind load docker-image shop-api:dev --name shop
> ```

### What just happened?

* The `Deployment` created a `ReplicaSet`, which created two pods.
  - each pod got a cluster-internal IP address
    + you can see them with `kubectl -n shop get pods -o wide`
  - the `api` Service load-balances across those addresses
* The `Ingress` routes requests for `shop.localtest.me` to the frontend Service.
  - the frontend calls the API through its Service name, `http://api:8080`
* The readiness probe keeps traffic away from pods that aren't ready yet.

## Step 5: Roll out a new version

1. Update the image:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n shop set image deployment/api api=ghcr.io/acme/sample-shop-api:2.4.0
   ```

2. Watch the rollout:

   - from a second terminal, run

         kubectl -n shop get pods -l app=api -w

     and keep it open; you'll see new pods start before the old ones terminate.
   - or simply run `kubectl -n shop rollout status deployment/api`.

3. If something goes wrong, roll back:

   ```bash
   kubectl -n shop rollout undo deployment/api
   ```

Expected output of `rollout status`:

```text
Waiting for deployment "api" rollout to finish: 1 out of 2 new replicas have been updated...
Waiting for deployment "api" rollout to finish: 1 old replicas are pending termination...
deployment "api" successfully rolled out
```

## Cleanup

Delete the whole cluster:

```bash
kind delete cluster --name shop
```

## Next steps

+ Add metrics with the [kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart](https://github.com/prometheus-community/helm-charts/tree/main/charts/kube-prometheus-stack#configuration).
+ Read about [rolling update parameters](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/#rolling-update-deployment) (`maxSurge`, `maxUnavailable`).
+ Try the same deployment on a managed cluster: see our guide at https://docs.acme.example.com/tutorials/sample-shop/managed-kubernetes?provider=all&step=1
+ Found a mistake in this tutorial? [Open an issue](https://github.com/acme/sample-shop/issues/new?labels=docs%2Ctutorial&template=docs_bug.md).

## Anatomy of a migration today

Here’s what renaming `customers.zip` to `customers.postal_code` looks like now. It’s three pull requests spread over about a week, and every one of them is boring on purpose:

1) **Expand.** Add the new column, plus a trigger that keeps both columns in sync while old and new code run side by side:

   ```sql
   ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN postal_code text;

   CREATE FUNCTION customers_sync_postal_code() RETURNS trigger AS $$
   BEGIN
     NEW.postal_code := COALESCE(NEW.postal_code, NEW.zip);
     NEW.zip         := COALESCE(NEW.zip, NEW.postal_code);
     RETURN NEW;
   END $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
   ```

2) **Migrate.** Backfill in batches, deploy the code that reads `postal_code`, and watch the dashboards for a day or two.
3) **Contract.** Drop the trigger, then — one release later, once we’re _really_ sure nothing reads it any more — drop `zip`.

The runner config that enforces the guard rails is tiny:

```yaml
# migrations/runner.yaml
lock_timeout: 2s
statement_timeout: 15m
retries: { max: 5, jitter: true }
checks:
  - invalid_indexes
  - unvalidated_constraints
  - table_rewrites
```
